title: The Association Between Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Postoperative Delirium: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
text: BACKGROUND: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent and serious complication following surgery, particularly in high-risk patients such as those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The relationship between COPD and the development of POD remains unclear, with existing studies providing inconsistent findings. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the association between COPD and postoperative delirium in surgical patients. METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, and other grey resources. Observational studies and randomized controlled trials assessing the incidence of POD in COPD patients were included. Data were extracted on study design, participant demographics, surgical context, and POD assessment. Both fixed-effect and random-effects models were evaluated, with model selection guided by statistical heterogeneity and study characteristics. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity. RESULTS: A total of 26 studies involving 43,051 patients were included. Both unadjusted and adjusted analyses showed a significant association between COPD and the increased risk of POD. The pooled odds ratio (OR) for the association in adjusted analyses was 2.08 (95% CI: 1.60-2.71, P < 0.001; I2 = 67.2%). In the adjusted subgroup analysis, the association remained statistically significant in non-cardiac surgery but did not reach statistical significance in cardiac surgery; however, the between-subgroup difference was not statistically significant (P for interaction = 0.139). Geographic variation was identified as a potential effect modifier, with studies conducted in Asia showing a stronger association. CONCLUSION: The available evidence suggests an association between COPD and higher odds of POD in surgical patients, including in studies reporting multivariable-adjusted estimates. However, the predominantly observational evidence and between-study heterogeneity warrant cautious interpretation and do not establish causality. These findings highlight the potential importance of tailored perioperative management strategies for patients with COPD, although their effectiveness in reducing POD risk requires further investigation. Further well-designed prospective studies are necessary to confirm these findings and explore the underlying mechanisms. However, insufficient data on COPD severity precluded an assessment of whether this association varied across GOLD stages.
author_name: Zhenlin Wang, Jinhui Xu, Yufan Xi et al.

extra.journal: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

title: Inhaled Corticosteroids and Sickle Cell Disease Severity in Adults Without Asthma: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
text: IMPORTANCE: People living with sickle cell disease (SCD) who have episodic cough and wheeze (ECW) without a diagnosis of asthma have high rates of pain episodes and acute chest syndrome. A previous trial, in which patients with SCD and ECW without asthma received 15 weeks of inhaled mometasone or placebo, showed that inhaled mometasone improved daily pain and reduced soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1), a marker of disease severity in SCD. OBJECTIVE: To examine the biologic effects and safety of long-term daily inhaled mometasone in patients without asthma but with SCD and ECW. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial recruited patients with SCD from December 2018 to May 2022. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either inhaled mometasone or placebo for 48 weeks. Data analyses followed the modified intention-to-treat principle and were performed between July and November 2023. INTERVENTIONS: The inhaled mometasone group received 220 μg of inhaled mometasone furoate dry powder once daily. The placebo group received a matching placebo inhaler. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was percentage change in soluble VCAM-1 levels from baseline to end of study. Secondary outcomes included laboratory results, functional outcomes, patient-reported outcomes, and health care utilization. RESULTS: Of the 77 patients who received the intervention and were included in the analysis, 40 were assigned to inhaled mometasone (mean [SD] age, 36.0 [11.6] years; 26 females [65%]) and 37 were assigned to placebo (mean [SD] age, 31.5 [8.6] years; 19 males [51%]). Compared with the placebo group, the inhaled mometasone group increased their soluble VCAM-1 levels by 42% (95% CI, -11% to 96%; P = .02). Point estimates for clinical outcomes favored the placebo group, although the findings were not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this trial of adults with SCD and ECW, extended courses of inhaled mometasone were associated with worsened markers of disease severity. Inhaled mometasone should not be used long-term in patients with SCD and ECW without a definitive diagnosis of asthma. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03758950.
author_name: Susanna A Curtis, Sarah McCuskee, Robyn T Cohen et al.

text:
This Veterans Day, honoring those who served also means ensuring they receive the care, benefits, and recognition they have earned.

Hear from Victoria Paul, a Justice Catalyst Fellow here at the Lawyers’ Committee as she examines how race-based medical practices, including race-based spirometry, may impact how veterans’ respiratory disabilities are evaluated and compensated.

Spirometry is a common pulmonary function test that measures how much and the speed of air a person can breathe in and out, helping assess lung function and identify respiratory conditions. Historically, race-based adjustments in these tests have determined how lung function is interpreted, potentially affecting one’s access to appropriate care and disability benefits.

Veterans deserve fair, equitable treatment—not medical standards shaped by outdated racial assumptions.

As we honor those who served, we must also demand accountability and work toward a system that recognizes and protects every veteran.

#VeteransDay #CivilRights #HealthEquity #VeteransRights #RaceBasedMedicine

title: Associations between temperatures, extreme temperature events, and onset of acute exacerbations of COPD: a time-stratified case-crossover study in China.
text: BACKGROUND: Non-optimal temperatures and extreme temperature events may trigger acute exacerbations of COPD (AECOPD), but most evidence is admission based, potentially misclassifying exposure timing and obscuring susceptible groups. RESEARCH QUESTION: Are non-optimal temperature and extreme temperature events associated with AECOPD onset, and which patients are most susceptible? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We used the Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Registry (ACURE) data and assigned residential temperature exposure using ERA5-Land, a reanalysis dataset of European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Cold spells (CS) were defined as consecutive days below location-specific low-temperature thresholds, and compound cold spells (CCS) as concurrent daytime and nighttime cold spells. Associations with reported symptom onset were estimated using a time-stratified case-crossover design, conditional logistic regression with distributed lag nonlinear models. Subgroup and cytokine analyses assessed susceptibility and inflammation. RESULTS: Among 5,634 patients with AECOPD (mean age, 69.4 ± 9.5 years; 78.8% male), lower temperature was associated with higher odds of AECOPD onset, whereas higher temperature was not. The strongest associations occurred for CS lasting ≥3 days and CCS lasting ≥2 days over lag 0-3 days, with ORs of 1.84 (95% CI, 1.22-2.78) and 4.31 (95% CI, 2.07-8.97), respectively. Nearly half had delayed admission within 14 days. Using admission rather than onset dates attenuated estimates by 88.8% for CS and 84.8% for CCS. Associations were stronger among older adults, men, smokers, patients with severe AECOPD in the past year or previously diagnosed COPD, and those using combination inhaler in the preceding year. CS were also associated with higher TNF-α, IL-6, and CXCL-11 concentrations. INTERPRETATION: Lower temperature and extreme cold events, particularly CCS, were associated with AECOPD onset. Symptom-onset timing may better capture temperature-related associations than admission timing. These findings highlight the need for targeted cold-weather prevention strategies to reduce AECOPD burden. TRIAL REGISTRY: ClinicalTrials.gov; NO.: NCT02657525.
author_name: Changyun Zhang, Hailu Zhu, Zhaoyang Pan et al.
